extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, poets, and readers interested in literary theory and the philosophy of art
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Plato's criteria for judging poetry and imitation: whether poetry conveys truth or mere appearance, whether the poet possesses knowledge of what he depicts, and the effects of imitative art on soul and city. Useful for evaluating poetic works and their ethical/educational value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of imitative poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: All poetical imitations are ruinous to the understanding of the hearers and therefore ought not to be received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato asserts this as a rule of the ideal State: imitative poetry should be rejected because it misleads the soul. The text frames this as a clear policy decision grounded in the prior account of the parts of the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is imitation (thrice removed from truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is an imitator and therefore (like a painter) is thrice removed from the truth: there is the ideal/form (God's bed), the maker (carpenter), and the imitator (painter/poet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the bed example, Plato distinguishes three levels of production and emphasizes that poets copy appearances, not realities. This structural criterion devalues works that merely reproduce surface appearance rather than engaging with Forms or realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitators lack genuine knowledge of their subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitative artists (poets, painters) do not possess the true knowledge of the things they represent; they only know appearances and cannot claim expertise in the practical arts they depict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a painter may paint a cobbler without understanding cobbling; a poet may speak of military tactics or politics but lacks the practical knowledge to be a legislator or commander. This criterion judges artistic authority by whether the creator knows the underlying practice, not merely its appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real art seeks realities rather than images
rubrics_metrics.description: The true artist or maker, if able to make originals as well as images, would prefer to make realities and be concerned with truth instead of devoting himself to imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato argues that a maker who truly understands would not choose image-making as life's pursuit; the genuine craftsman aims at producing real, useful things and lasting memorials, not merely flattering appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate by maker/user/imitator roles (use determines excellence)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three arts concerning any thing: the user (who has knowledge), the maker (who makes the thing), and the imitator (who paints or represents it); excellence of a thing is relative to its use and the user is the authority on goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the flute-player (user) knows better than the flute-maker which flutes are good; the imitator lacks the user's experiential knowledge. Therefore assess poetic depiction by reference to the practical use it represents and whether the depiction aligns with that use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's educative and civic efficacy as a criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's worth may be judged by whether his work actually educates or improves individuals or cities; Homer, for example, is criticized for not having made any city better or acting as a legislator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato challenges the claim that poets are teachers of virtue by asking for evidence of poets' practical benefit to society (laws, successful counsel, schools of followers). Art that fails to contribute to civic improvement is suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation appeals to appearance and deceives through form
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody, rhythm, and the colours of language can mask lack of knowledge; imitation deceives the ignorant by making appearances seem like realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strip away music and metre and many poetical tales appear poor; thus evaluate works for whether stylistic features obscure substantive ignorance. Beware of audiences who judge solely by pleasing appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is a form of play, not serious knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic imitation is characterized as 'play or sport'—a superficial laying on of colours—rather than the expression of true knowledge about the subjects it treats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion distinguishes between seriousness/epistemic status: works intended as imitation should not be granted the authority of knowledge. Critics should treat imitative works accordingly and not conflate rhetorical skill with expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of pleasure and truth in aesthetic judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures derived from imitation (especially bodily pleasures mediated by senses) are inferior, mixed with pains and shadows of true pleasure; truer pleasures are those aligned with reason and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato links aesthetic value to moral and epistemic truth: when evaluating art, consider whether the pleasures it offers lead the soul toward reason and truth or merely flatter base appetites. This grounds aesthetic judgment in ethical and ontological criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance from reason/order as a measure of artistic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Works and desires farther removed from reason, law, and order are less aligned with true pleasure and truth; the more distant the artist's subject or method is from reason, the more illusive and deceptive the pleasure it offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this as an axis: rank works by their proximity to reason and orderly truth. Imitative works that reinforce unruly passions or false images score low on this metric, while works that cultivate order and the rational parts of the soul score higher.
